						Glastonbury 2025 Saturday: Neil Young competes with Charli XCX
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/music/news/g.text:
With his 1972 song Old Man currently the toast of TikTok, one wonders whether Neil Young is due the kind of resurgence experienced in recent years by Fleetwood Mac and Creedence Clearwater Revival. He’s got the hits. He’s got the endearing curmudgeon personality (and the liberal politics). He’s got the famous friends. Will tonight’s televised performance help to ramp up interest, or are all the young people too busy live-streaming Charli? Poppie Platt
Have we ever had such a striking contrast of styles and generational tastes at Glastonbury? The Other stage might as well be in a different universe to the Pyramid.
Charli is working her crowd like a pro – and the audience at home too. She has just suggestively backed up towards the camera and then smouldered down the lens.
Mind, she hasn’t given us a harmonica solo yet...
She did NOT get the plaid memo. Charli is in black leather pants and a crop top, sunglasses on, a giant brat screen behind her. She gyrates and wiggles her behind at the audience and they obligingly go wild.
James Hall writes: She’s here. After The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony warms up the crowd, lights around the Other stage start strobing and Charli’s image and name flash up on the screens to throbbing bass. A curtain falls to reveal the green brat logo, and Charli bounds on to 365. “Party Girl” flashes on the screens. “F---ing jump!” she screams. And so we all do. She’s brought the party, and the word-perfect crowd are up for it.
If Neil is putting you to sleep, fire up BBC One. There are flashing screens! Propulsive beats! The promise of fashion that isn’t gently rumpled! Charli XCX is due any minute...
And we’re in. I just spoke to a member of the crowd-controlling team beside the Other stage who told me they have no concerns for overcrowding here this evening – she assures me each spoke that feeds into this area has its own crew ensuring things don’t get out of hand. That said, this crowd is so massive it’s pretty clear Charli could have filled the Pyramid stage without issue... Hope the Neil Young fans are enjoying their personal space over there. LA Robinson
Have some of the Neil fans ended up at Charli XCX’s show? There are lots of middle-aged men, with and without teenage daughters. I’ve even spotted one with “prat” in the iconic album font on a green shirt. She isn’t only doing it for the girls. Lauren Shirreff
Over on the Young broadcast, I’m really quite mesmerised by the amount of denim and plaid on that stage. It’s like a lumberjack convention.
The normally free-flowing Glastonbury – whereby punters can move around anytime, any place, anywhere – has hit a serious snag. People’s enormous desire to see Charli XCX and the Scissor Sisters has led to the closure of access to the Woodsies tent (Scissor Sisters) and the Other stage (Charli), at least from one side in the latter’s case.
The joy of Glasto is the ability to go to anything whenever you want. Not tonight, it seems. Is it simply a case of too many ticket-holders? Or have organisers put the wrong names on the wrong stages? James Hall
Poppie Platt, who’s actually on the ground, takes a slightly different view.
Neil Young’s set opened with little fanfare: no fancy lights or elaborate staging in sight. He stood, alone, strumming out Sugar Mountain, the rapt crowd almost silent as it waited for him to break into his extended harmonica solo. Second track Be the Rain ramped the energy up slightly, and also heralded the arrival of Young’s band, the Chrome Hearts, on stage.
But this is very much a man and his instruments – namely, the type of Glastonbury set you’d have got 50 years ago, before the Pyramid stage headline slot became an event designed for television. And, one imagines, the antithesis of what Charli (hardly known for her love of singing live) is bringing to the Other right now.
Those Young superfans aside, it’s not the most dynamic concert experience thus far – at least not from the broadcast. Young’s face is in shadow thanks to his baseball cap, there are no performance fireworks (literal or otherwise), and the crowd sound content rather than delirious.
A reminder that Young’s flip-flopping over whether he’d allow the BBC to broadcast his set at all means that Charli XCX will get the prime BBC One slot shortly, while Young, after making a late concession, has to make do with BBC Two.

“Is all the green for Charli or for Neil?” a midlife man asks his friend as he heads towards the Pyramid stage. It’s a valid question: he may have drawn a thin crowd, with more people heading away from the stage than to it, but the old(er) rockers are very much out for Neil Young tonight.
Peter Langerak, 70, was brought to Glastonbury from Auckland by his daughter for his big birthday and is buzzing, even though he’s been going since 11am. He saw Young once “so long ago that I can’t remember” and is especially excited to for his set, but adds:“I’m enjoying everything.”
Steve Hunt, 56, saw Young play the Pyramid stage all the way back in 2009, so “I thought I’d come back and see him again,” he says. Back then “he was good, and he’s a bit of a legend, so you don’t get a chance to see him very often,” says Steve. “I think he’ll play all the big hits, like Harvest Moon, so it’ll be a good night.” He’s personally hoping for Like a Hurricane. Lauren Shirreff

						Farage pledges to reopen Welsh coal mines - watch live
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
We are expecting Nigel Farage to be on his feet in Port Talbot to deliver his speech just after noon.
You will be able to watch the address live at the top of this page.
Labour has held power in the Senedd since its inception in 1999.
In 2021 the party won 30 of the 60 seats available. The Tories were a distant second with 16 seats and Plaid Cymru finished in third place with 13.
The Liberal Democrats secured just one seat.
Reform currently has zero representatives in the Welsh Parliament but the party is hoping to change that at the elections due to be held in May next year.
Reform is riding high in the national opinion polls and the party believes it has a chance of winning power in Wales in 2026.
The Port Talbot plant in south Wales was, until recently, the UK’s largest steel-maker.
But Tata Steel, the Indian firm that runs it, announced last year that the remaining blast furnaces would be closed, leading to the loss of up to 2,800 jobs at the site.
The blast furnaces are being replaced with an electric arc furnace, which will produce less steel but in a more eco-friendly way. It will not be fully operational until 2028.
Nigel Farage is expected to say that he wants Port Talbot’s blast furnaces to reopen in the long run, while admitting the outcome would not be easy to achieve.
It is a big day for Nigel Farage and Reform UK as the party leader steps up his attempts to win power at the 2026 Senedd elections and attempts to draw a line under the Zia Yusuf row.
Mr Farage will deliver a speech in Port Talbot at noon and he will vow to reopen the town’s blast furnaces if his party wins power.
He will also say that Reform would allow Welsh coal mines to be brought back to life so that the domestic fuel could be used at the Port Talbot plant.
He told The Mail: “Our long-term aim is to hopefully reopen Port Talbot steelworks – and instead of importing coal for it, use our own.”
Reform is targeting success at the Welsh Parliament elections in May next year and Mr Farage is putting steel-making at the heart of his party’s campaign.
Mr Farage will be keen to use today’s address to move on from the party feuding that led Mr Yusuf to quit as Reform’s chairman on Thursday only for him to return to the frontline in a new role on Saturday.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/06.title: What’s wrong with a £30 million wedding? Bezos has done Venice a favour
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/06.subtitle: The Amazon CEO is absolutely within his rights to take over the city for his nuptials in as vulgar and showy a way as he chooses
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/06.text:
One gathers from insiders, business journalists and whistleblowers that Amazon offers a workplace that is, shall we say, challenging at best. The company’s culture is, of course, that bestowed by its CEO Jeff Bezos, one of the richest men in the world.
Bezos and MacKenzie Scott, an intelligent, impressive and decent-seeming woman – who helped Bezos found Amazon – divorced as he pursued his affair with TV anchor Lauren Sanchez, a busty Latina known for her vaulting ambition and enormous personality.
The Amazon CEO is a changed man with Sanchez: he’s got himself a decent set of abs and a new wardrobe. The pair canoodles constantly in public, showing the world their love (and lust). The weekend saw them host a foam party aboard Bezos’s yacht moored off Croatia. It was allegedly for Sanchez’s son’s birthday, but that didn’t stop the lip-locked pair stealing the attention with their own lustful antics.
Their €48m wedding this week in Venice reflects their outsize passion. Due to take place at the Scuola Grande della Misericordia, a 16th-century compound in the centre, it has attracted all the loathing and disruption you might imagine. Protesters from a group called No Space for Bezos threatened to fill the canal with inflatable crocodiles and thus block arriving guests. As Tommaso Cacciari, a member of the No Space for Bezos protest group, put it: “This is a big victory for us. Who would have thought that we could change the plans of one of the richest men on the planet?”
The victory is limited, however, with the ceremony merely moved to the Arsenale, an even more glorious venue, and one with crenelated walls and a drawbridge that will be better at keeping protesters out. Venice Marco Polo is a traffic jam of private jets. Guests from Diane von Furstenberg to Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump have already arrived, looking hot (as in sweaty).
Of course one can sympathise with the natural antipathy many feel towards a wedding like this. Bezos is not a likeable character, the wedding is hardly a fairytale sort of romance, and at a moment of extreme income inequality, Amazon’s evasive tax practices, while legal, do sit badly.
Even so, Bezos is absolutely within his rights to take over Venice for his nuptials in as vulgar and showy a way as he chooses. Yes, the cost of the week’s celebrations alone could save many lives less fortunate, but tough cheese. It’s his money and he can do with it as he pleases.
Indeed, those against the wedding are simply falling prey to the old European antipathy to wealth, especially American wealth, a hatred so extreme that many in the bloc are willing to be the poorer for it. Spain’s anti-tourism antics, which include cracking down on Airbnb and second homes, show as much.
The truth is that Venice, like most Mediterranean cities, would be completely lost without its income from foreigners, the wealthier the better. The main home-grown economy now is tourism and the money that people spend on hotels and everything else when in town for the film festival, the Biennale, and of course the holidays is their lifeline; the Covid lockdown nearly ruined Italy by keeping tourists out and restaurants partially shut. Venice’s own costs are precipitously rising due to the rising sea level. It is the most expensive city on earth to renovate. Bezos’s wedding will provide much-needed cash to the city and locals alike.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: British manufacturing is dying before our eyes
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: Labour needs to take bold action to lower energy costs in this week’s industrial strategy
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
British industry has hit a new low. Factories consumed the least energy in 50 years in 2024, with the decline almost entirely because of shutdowns and closures.
Factory bosses say Britain’s sky-high energy costs are crippling heavy industry, forcing businesses to shut down production lines or abandon operations altogether. They blame surging gas prices but also a succession of green levies piled onto bills.
The energy consumption slump, spelt out in the latest government statistics, comes just days before the Government is expected to announce its new industrial strategy. Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, is pledging to reverse decades of decline.
But the energy consumption data – widely seen as a proxy for the state of British manufacturing, especially the energy-intensive sectors – suggests Reynolds will need some truly radical measures if he is to succeed.
Britain has millions of businesses, which all consume energy, but what such data reflects most strongly are the trends within our “foundational industries” – energy-intensive manufacturing that produces the basic materials other sectors need to function.
This includes steel, cement, chemicals, glass, paper and ceramics. Production of all of these materials relies on cheap, plentiful heat.
If that heat becomes expensive, those industries die – and that, both the stats and the industries themselves say, is what is happening.
Take glass: the sector is facing “the worst situation I have witnessed in 45 years in the industry”, says Dave Dalton, the British Glass chief executive. “We will have the lowest output of glass for nearly 50 or 60 years.”
Britain’s heavy industries are being wiped out by surging energy costs, driven partly by global gas markets, but also by the lethal addition of green levies and excessive transmission charges that leave UK companies with the world’s biggest energy bills.
“Our industry is on its knees,” said Stuart Collings, the chief executive of Ineos Olefins and Polymers, which has plants in Runcorn, Teesside and Grangemouth. “UK chemical companies are losing money, and many can barely afford to maintain plants. And energy costs are the key reason.”
His warning follows last month’s announcement that one of Britain’s biggest chemical plants, the Sabic Olefins “cracker” facility in Teesside, faces closure due to concerns over spiralling energy prices.
Many other similar facilities have already gone. CF Fertilisers shut down its ammonia plants in Billingham and Chester in 2023, citing “projected high natural gas prices”.
Ineos has also suffered, with owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe warning that soaring energy costs and levies will drive the UK’s multibillion-pound chemicals industry into “extinction”. Last January he shut down the UK’s final bioethanol plant, sited at Grangemouth, next door to the Ineos Refinery that also had to close recently.
Grangemouth’s remaining Ineos plant turns oil and gas into plastic feedstocks, but Collings warns that energy costs, levies and other charges are squeezing too hard.
“We make ethylene, which is the building block of the chemical and plastics industries, but we are paying really high energy costs, partly because of all the green levies on energy and partly because we have to buy carbon credits against the CO2 we emit.
“And we are competing against companies in America and elsewhere whose products can be imported without any of those taxes.”
Hundreds of other companies rely on the UK petrochemicals industry for the feedstocks needed to make their own products – everything from carpets and sofas to the insulation around our domestic wiring.
Other foundational industries face exactly the same problems. The latest report from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) spells out how industrial electricity costs have risen from 14.8p per kilowatt hour in January 2021 to 26.0p at the end of 2024 – a 75pc rise.
Similarly, industrial gas prices have more than doubled from 2.5p per kilowatt hour to 5.5p over the same period.
Even over that very short period, those high energy prices – which are up to five times greater than in the US and three times higher than in the EU – have had a devastating impact, driving the output of energy-intensive industries down by 33pc.
“Collectively, the volume of output in these industries has fallen by one third since the start of 2021, and is now at its lowest level since the start of the available time series in 1990,” the ONS said.
The metals industry has been hardest hit, with output now around half of what it was in 2021. Petrochemicals and paper products are down by a third. The ceramics industry fell by “only” 20pc.
The high price of gas on European markets is contributing to the death of British industry. But it is only one of three key factors.
Another, perhaps the most important, is the multitude of government-imposed green levies and taxes put on companies, such as the climate change levy, renewables obligation, feed-in tariffs and so on.
On top of this, UK companies also face higher network charges – the cost for the pipes and cables – than elsewhere. These are up to 90pc higher than in Europe.
For policymakers there is a sliver of good news buried in such tough figures. Although they cannot control the price of gas, they can control levies, taxes and network costs.
In ceramics, another hard-hit sector, it’s too late to save the likes of Royal Stafford, a pottery firm with a 200-year history, or Johnson Tiles’ factory, also in Stoke-on-Trent, both of which shut down last year.
“The cost of making tiles in this country has become increasingly unsustainable,” Johnson director Stephen Dixon told the BBC at the time.
Robert Flello, the chief executive of trade body Ceramics UK, said successive governments had pursued decarbonisation by deindustrialisation, “hammering UK industry while allowing imports from countries that still burn coal and which have poor emissions and environmental standards.”
He is pinning his hopes on the industrial strategy offering a complete rewrite on energy. In particular, he wants ceramics producers admitted to the existing Energy Intensive Industries scheme – dubbed the British Industry Supercharger by the last government – which exempts them from many of Ed Miliband’s green levies.
This would cut costs but not by enough, so he also wants the UK’s planned carbon border adjustment mechanism extended to ceramics. This is a levy taking effect in 2027 that will put a carbon price on imported cement, fertilisers and steel, theoretically making some imports more expensive to stop them undercutting British industry.
Such hopes are echoed by manufacturers of both cement and glass, two other key products for thousands of other UK businesses.
Diana Casey, who oversees the cement and lime industries at the Mineral Products Association, said the UK must match European countries in support for energy-intensive industries and impose a carbon tax on imports.
“We urgently have to get UK industrial electricity prices in line with other nations, or domestic production will never be competitive.
“UK companies face electricity bills nearly three times higher than in the US, and almost double those in France or Germany. This stifles inward investment and competitiveness, and means the domestic industry is being replaced by imports.”
The GMB Union, which is among Labour’s most loyal supporters and funders, has told Labour a major rethink on energy is essential – warning that at current rates of decline the UK will soon be unable even to manufacture the kit needed for its own energy networks.
Andy Prendergast, the GMB national secretary, said: “The GMB believes the existing energy and industrial policy trajectory is putting the cart before the horse. We are sprinting to clean power without the manufacturing and skills capacities even to win the contracts and jobs supporting that transition.”
British industry’s last hope of reversing the devastating declines of recent years rests almost entirely on the Government taking bold action to lower energy costs in this week’s industrial strategy.
Will that happen? The green paper consultation document published by Reynolds last February is not encouraging. It reiterated Labour’s commitment to green energy as a solution, rather than a cause, for high prices.
“High electricity costs are a major barrier to growth and investment,” it said. “The only way to guarantee our energy security and protect bill payers is to speed up the transition away from fossil fuels and towards home-grown clean energy.”
Manufacturers fear that sentence implies they will face even more of the levies and subsidies essential to make renewable energy viable.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: Skoda electric car sales overtake Tesla in Europe after Musk backlash
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: Continent continues to shun EV maker in protest against billionaire’s support for Donald Trump
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
Skoda has overtaken Tesla for electric vehicle (EV) sales in Europe as motorists continue to shun Elon Musk’s carmaker in protest against his support for Donald Trump.
Tesla’s total sales across the Continent fell by 28pc to 14,055 in May, according to market research firm DataForce, which were lower than Skoda’s EV monthly tally of 14,920.
The shift was fuelled largely by the ongoing boycott against Tesla in Europe, although Skoda’s popularity also surged after the launch of its electric Elroq SUV model, which accounted for 9,250 sales in May.
Tesla’s declining popularity could also be seen in separate figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, which revealed that the company’s sales in the UK and Europe fell for the fifth successive month in May.
It found that just 8,729 new Teslas were registered last month, down 40.5pc year-on-year.
That was despite overall EV sales in Europe rising by 27.2pc over the period, accounting for 193,493 vehicles in total.
This increase was also reflected in the UK, where electric car sales were up by 25.8pc in May.
As well as coping with the political backlash, Mr Musk’s company has also been battling mounting competition from Chinese rivals attempting to flood Europe with cheaper cars.
This led to Tesla posting a 13pc drop in global sales during the first three months of 2025, reflecting its worst quarter since 2022.
Investors have grown increasingly concerned over the impact of Mr Musk’s politics in recent months, as his support for Right-wing political leaders scared off swathes of potential buyers.
Earlier this month, a group of French drivers went as far as suing Tesla over claims that Mr Musk has turned their cars into totems of the “extreme-Right”.
In the UK, Tesla’s sales also dropped by 36pc in May, according to data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.
That was in stark contrast to BYD, the Chinese carmaker behind the cut-price Dolphin Surf, which saw monthly sales rise by more than 400pc to hit 3,025 cars sold.
Tesla’s share price has fallen by 10pc so far this year, although it has erased some of its losses after Mr Musk stepped down from a role in the White House last month and vowed to refocus on Tesla.
Mr Musk has increasingly pinned Tesla’s future on self-driving technology, launching a driverless robotaxi service in Austin, Texas on Sunday. The company is also developing a humanoid robot called Optimus.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: How inflation is killing off the pint
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: Smaller-sized measures are creeping on to drinks menus as pubs battle to get punters through the door
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
Nothing is as emblematic of Britain’s drinking culture as the pint. For hundreds of years, the imperial measure has been served in the nation’s pubs.
Yet as inflation pushes the price of a pint to record highs, smaller servings are increasingly being poured across the country.
Pub owners say they are selling more beer in so-called “schooner” glasses, which hold two thirds of a pint, because drinkers are striving to keep the cost of a night out under control.
“Nowadays, two thirds are becoming a little bit more popular in general, regardless of what the beer style is,” says Gabor Csupity, of the Friendship Pub Company, which runs a string of pubs in London.
“I think there is a simple answer to [why] which is the price of beer.”
It raises the question: could the pint be facing extinction in Britain’s pubs?
The cost of a pint has soared across Britain in recent years, with the average rising above £5 nationally for the first time this year. In many pubs it is already pushing £7. In London, £8 pints are not uncommon.
Hospitality companies have had to grapple with surging energy bills and skyrocketing labour costs – including higher National Insurance (NI) bills levied on them by Rachel Reeves in her maiden Budget – making price rises inevitable.
Big chains such as JD Wetherspoon have been able to keep their prices lower by using their scale to leverage better deals with brewers. But most smaller groups and independent pubs have been forced to pay a much higher price to keep the beer flowing.
It has left many trying to come up with more creative ways to stop customers baulking at the price of a drink.
“We’re familiar with holding pint glasses so holding a half pint just doesn’t quite feel right,” says Mark Dredge, beer expert and author. “Whereas now, you get the schooner, it feels natural still, and you don’t feel like you’re getting less.”
James Ratcliffe, co-owner of The Black Bull in Sedbergh, Cumbria, says: “We’ve started [selling schooners] now, it keeps the spend down a little bit for people. It’s a bit more than a half, but it’s not quite at full price – it keeps the price a bit more reasonable.”
Mr Csupity also sees it as a way of ensuring that buying a few rounds of drinks each week stays accessible. “People still want to be in a pub and still want to have a beer. If you’re just having that two thirds, maybe five of those once a week, you’ve already saved £8 or £9, easily,” he says.
Though famously popular in Australia, for many years a “schooner” was banned in British pubs. Landlords were unable to serve them owing to historic laws dating back to the 1600s to stop drinkers being short-changed with short drinks.
However, these rules were relaxed by the Government in 2011 in response to the rise of craft beers, many of which were stronger than ales and lagers, warranting a smaller pour. The change allowed pubs to pour two thirds pints alongside full measures and halves.
“From a business perspective, schooners allow bars to serve high-ABV or more expensive beers in a size that keeps price points accessible,” says Tony Barron, supply chain manager at BrewDog, which lobbied the Government in favour of loosening the rules.
“There’s less waste, more flexibility and a better drinking experience – particularly if the customer wants to try multiple beers in one visit, and especially if they are a bit of a beer connoisseur.”
Until recently the schooner remained a quirk found in craft bars and specialist pubs. But the cost of living crisis means it’s now creeping on to more and more menus.
Barron says: “This isn’t just about craft beer and craft beer drinkers any more – lagers and even stouts are getting the schooner treatment. Our take is that this reflects a steady but significant shift in British drinking culture.”
Nico Treguer, co-founder of the Culpeper Family Hospitality group, says: “There are actually a multitude of personal preferences driving this demand, from wanting to try various beer profiles including some with higher ABV over a pub session to wanting to spend less due to cost of living pressures.”
Social media has also played a role, with accounts such as the Schooner Scorer, bringing exposure to the smaller-sized drink.
Yet while the schooner has its advocates, some worry that customers could end up getting less than they bargained for if they do not pay careful attention to what they are being charged.
“The rise of the schooner seems to be about making pricing feel more palatable to customers – but ultimately, it’s a smaller measure for what often feels like the same price,” says David Hattersley, owner of the Old Exeter Inn in Devon, who does not sell the measure.
“From a publican’s point of view, it reflects the wider economic pressures we’re under. With increasing costs, taxation, and supply challenges, we’re all having to adapt.”
However, he adds: “It’s not unlike shrinking a chocolate bar but keeping the packaging the same.”
Andy Kerr, owner of The Sun Tavern in Bethnal Green, London, says: “I have seen in certain places that they don’t tell you it’s two thirds of a pint, and they’re charging you the same as a pint. That’s when it’s a bit sly.”
Mr Csupity has also seen some less scrupulous publicans using smaller measures as a way to charge higher prices by stealth.
“In some places you go in and it’s £6 for a pint but you pay £3.50 for a half – I always find that silly,” he says.
He says Friendship Pubs’ venues make sure to serve schooners on a “mathematically bang-on” basis so customers aren’t short-changed, meaning if you would be paying £6 for any particular pint, a schooner will be £4.
It will likely be some time before drinkers truly adopt the schooner en masse. Ratcliffe says so far he has only introduced schooners for the more expensive beers in his pub, although he is open to using them more broadly in future.
“I don’t see why not – we’re just experimenting with it at the moment and people are getting their heads around it,” he says. “It will take a little bit of time, but for those that do, once it clicks, it clicks.”
What does it mean for the fate of the pint? Beer expert Dredge warns that unless something changes radically on energy costs and taxes, the measure could become a much rarer sight.
“Beer is expensive nowadays, and it’s not going to get cheaper. You’re probably paying now the same for a schooner as you did for a pint a few years ago.
“And if that’s the case, then rather than changing your habits, you can just change your glass, so you can just take that little step down.”
author: Daniel Woolfson
